## Overview

The American Community Survey is the Census Bureau's annual nationwide
survey of U.S. households, reaching roughly 3.5 million addresses each
year with a mandatory questionnaire covering demographics, housing,
economics, and social characteristics. The ACS contributes a people-and-households layer to rural analysis that
administrative data cannot. Where datasets like QCEW and BDS describe
jobs, establishments, employment, and wages, ACS adds the characteristics
of the people and households behind those measures: education, income,
occupation, housing, commuting patterns, internet access, and
work-from-home rates. For any analysis that asks not just "how many
jobs" but "who holds them, at what pay, and under what conditions," ACS
is where the answer lives.

The survey produces two main products. **1-year estimates** cover
geographies with populations of 65,000 or more and are released each
fall for the prior calendar year — current, but limited in geographic
reach. **5-year estimates** aggregate five years of survey data and are
available for all geographies including small counties, census tracts,
block groups, and places — making them the essential product for rural
analysis, where most counties fall below the 1-year threshold. The
trade-off is currency: 5-year estimates represent a rolling average, not
a snapshot of a single year.

## What This Data Tells Us About Rural America

The ACS provides the broadest cross-section of socioeconomic conditions
at the county level — covering educational attainment, income,
employment by occupation, housing costs, work-from-home rates,
self-employment, and race and ethnicity. It is the primary federal
source for the demographic and household-level context that labor market
and business data alone cannot supply.

For rural analysis, ACS is particularly valuable for measures that
reflect the quality and accessibility of economic opportunity, not just
its quantity. Educational attainment shapes the workforce available to
attract and grow businesses. ACS measures self-employment but does not
distinguish opportunity entrepreneurship from necessity entrepreneurship
— drawing that distinction requires reading ACS alongside employment and
wage data. The share of workers working from home, paired with FCC
broadband coverage data, helps researchers explore whether infrastructure
availability is translating into workforce flexibility. These are
dimensions of economic conditions that QCEW and BDS cannot see.

The ACS can be accessed through [`tidycensus`](https://walker-data.com/tidycensus/),
an easy-to-use R package developed and maintained by Kyle Walker that provides a clean
interface to the Census Data API. Because an excellent tool already
exists, CORI does not maintain a separate ACS package. The Data Verse surfaces ACS as a key rural data
resource because understanding what it measures and how to use it well
in a rural context is part of what this resource is for.

## Coverage

- **Geography:** Nation, State, County, Census Tract, Block Group,
  Place, ZCTA, and more
- **Time range:** 1-year estimates: 2005–present; 5-year estimates:
  2009–present
- **Update frequency:** Annual; 1-year estimates typically released each
  September, 5-year estimates typically each December
- **Universe:** Varies by table; most tables cover the U.S. civilian
  noninstitutionalized population. Group quarters population is included
  for many subjects.

::: callout-note
**1-year vs. 5-year for rural analysis:** 1-year estimates are only
available for geographies with 65,000+ residents — which excludes most
rural counties. For county-level rural analysis, **5-year estimates are
the correct product**. They cover all counties and geographies but
represent a rolling 5-year average rather than a single year, so
year-over-year changes should be interpreted carefully given overlapping
sample periods.
:::

::: callout-important
**Mind the margins of error.** ACS estimates are based on a sample
survey, so every estimate carries a margin of error. Uncertainty is
generally greater for smaller geographies and smaller population groups.
When comparing rural communities or measuring change over time, consider
the margin of error rather than treating the point estimate as an exact
count. Kyle Walker's [margins of error
vignette](https://walker-data.com/tidycensus/articles/margins-of-error.html)
is an excellent primer on working with ACS uncertainty in R.
:::

## Key Variables

The ACS covers hundreds of variables. The most analytically valuable
for rural economic analysis fall into four groups:

**Demographics**

- Age and sex distribution
- Race, Hispanic origin, and ethnicity
- Nativity and place of birth; year of entry
- Disability status
- Language spoken at home

**Education**

- Educational attainment (less than high school through graduate degree)
- School enrollment

**Employment, Income, and Economic Characteristics**

- Employment status and labor force participation
- Occupation and industry of employment
- Self-employment (incorporated and unincorporated)
- Remote work / work-from-home status
- Median household income; per capita income; poverty rate
- Earnings by sex and occupation

**Housing**

- Housing tenure (owner vs. renter)
- Median home value; median gross rent
- Housing cost burden (share of income spent on housing)
- Vacancy rate and vacancy type
- Internet access and subscription type
- Units in structure; year built

## Accessing the Data

`tidycensus` is the go-to R package for ACS data — and one of the best
data access tools in the R ecosystem, full stop. Written by Kyle Walker,
it wraps the Census Data API with a clean, consistent interface that
returns tidy data frames with geography attached, handles variable
lookups, and supports both 1-year and 5-year estimates across all
available geographies. If you are doing ACS analysis in R, start here.

```r
# install.packages("tidycensus")
library(tidycensus)

# Load ACS variable list for a given year
vars <- load_variables(2023, "acs5", cache = TRUE)

# Pull median household income for all counties (5-year estimates)
income <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = "B19013_001",   # median household income
  year      = 2023,
  survey    = "acs5"
)

# Pull multiple variables with geometry attached
edu <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(
    ba_plus  = "B15003_022",  # bachelor's degree
    total    = "B15003_001"   # total population 25+
  ),
  year      = 2023,
  survey    = "acs5",
  geometry  = TRUE            # returns sf object with county boundaries
)
```

The Census Data API is also accessible directly for users who prefer
Python, SQL, or other environments. See the [ACS data
portal](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/data.html) for
bulk downloads and the [ACS methodology
page](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/methodology.html) for
full documentation of survey design, sampling, and accuracy.

## Related

- **Dataset:** [Census Population Estimates
  Program](/datasets/census-population-estimates/) — annual population
  totals that provide the denominator for ACS-derived per-capita rates
- **Dataset:** [FCC Broadband Service
  Data](/datasets/fcc-broadband/) — infrastructure availability that
  pairs with ACS internet adoption and remote work measures
- **Dataset:** [QCEW Employment &
  Wages](/datasets/qcew-employment-wages/) — administrative employment
  data that complements ACS's household-level labor force picture
- **Package:** [ruraldefinitions](/packages/ruraldefinitions/) —
  rural/nonrural classifications for filtering and comparing ACS
  estimates across county types
